source_text: Curatur et paralyticus, et quidem in coetu, spectante populo. uidebit enim, inquit Esaias, populus sublimitatem domini et gloriam dei. quam sublimitatem et quam gloriam? conualescite, manus dimissae et genua dissoluta — hoc erit paralysis —; conualescite. ne timete, non otiose iterans (conualescite') nec uane subiungens 'ne timete', quoniam cum redintegratione membrorum uirium quoque repraesentationem pollicebatur: exurge et tolle grabattum tuum, simul et animi uigorem ad non timendos qui dicturi erant: quis dimittet peccata nisi solus deus? habes itaque iam et specialis medicinae dispunctam prophetiam et eorum, quae medicinam sunt secuta. pariter et dimissorem delictorum Christum recognosce apud eundem prophetam: quoniam, inquit in plurimis dimittet delicta eorum, et delicta nostra ipse auferet. nam et in primore ex ipsius domini persona: etsi fuerint delicta uestra tamquam roseum, uelut niuem exalbabo, etsi tamquam coccinum, uelut lanam exalbabo, in roseo sanguinem ostendens prophetarum, in coccino domini, ut clariorem. etiam Micheas de uenia delictorum: quis deus, quomodo tu? eximens iniquitates et praeteriens iniustitias residuis hereditatis tuae; et non tenuit in testimonium iram suam, quia t uoluit et misericordiae; auertet et miserebitur nostri; demerget delicta nostra et demerget in profundum maris peccata nostra. sed et si nihil tale in Christum fuisset praedicatum, haberem huius benignitatis exempla in creatore, promittentia mihi et in filio patris adfectus. uideo Niniuitas scelerum ueniam consecutos a creatore, ne dixerim tunc quoque a Christo, qui a primordio egit in patris nomine. lego et Nathan prophetam agnoscenti Dauid delictum suum in Uriam dixisse: et dominus circumduxit delictum tuum et non morieris; proinde et Achab regem, maritum Iezabel, reum idolatriae et sanguinis Nabuthae, ueniam meruisse paenitentiae nomine, (et) Ionathan, filium Saulis, resignati ieiunii culpam deprecatione delesse. quid de ipso populo retexam, totiens delictorum indulgentia restituto? ab eo scilicet deo, qui mauult misericordiam quam sacrificium et peccatoris paenitentiam quam mortem. prius est igitur, neges creatorem indulsisse aliquando delicta, consequens est, ut ostendas nec in Christum suum tale quid eum praedicasse: et ita probabis nouam istam Christi, noui scilicet, benignitatem, si probaueris nec parem creatori nec praedicatam a creatore. sed et peccata dimittere an eius possit esse, qui negetur tenere, et an eius sit absoluere, cuius non sit etiam damnare, et an congruat eum ignoscere, in quem nihil sit admissum, alibi iam congressi malumus admonere quam retractare.
pass_a_gloss: And a paralytic is healed, and indeed in a gathering, with the people watching. For Isaiah says, the people will see the loftiness of the Lord and the glory of God. What loftiness and what glory? Be strong, hands released and knees untied — this will be paralysis —; be strong. Do not fear, not idly repeating 'be strong' nor vainly adding 'do not fear', because with the restoration of limbs he was also promising a representation of strength: arise and take up your pallet, and at the same time, vigor of mind not to fear those who would say: who can forgive sins except God alone? You have, therefore, already a special medicine's distinct prophecy and those things which followed the medicine. Similarly, recognize Christ, the forgiver of sins, in the same prophet: for he says, in many places he will forgive their sins, and he will take away our sins. For also in the first, from the Lord's own person: if your sins are like scarlet, I will whiten them like snow, if they are like crimson, I will whiten them like wool, showing blood in scarlet, the Lord's in crimson, to make it clearer. And also Micah about the forgiveness of sins: what God is like you? taking away iniquities and passing over injustices to the remnant of your inheritance; and he did not retain his anger as a testimony, because he wanted mercy; he will turn away and have mercy on us; he will sink our sins and sink them into the depth of the sea. But even if nothing like this had been predicted about Christ, I would have examples of this kindness in the creator, promising to me also in the son the father's affections. I see the Ninevites having obtained forgiveness of sins from the creator, why should I not say also from Christ, who acted from the beginning in the father's name. I read also the prophet Nathan, recognizing David's sin in Uriah, saying: and the Lord has taken away your sin, and you will not die; and also King Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, guilty of idolatry and the blood of Naboth, having merited forgiveness by the name of repentance, and Jonathan, the son of Saul, having deleted the fault of resigned fasting by prayer. What about the people themselves, how often restored by forgiveness of sins? by that God, who prefers mercy to sacrifice and the repentance of the sinner to death. It is prior, therefore, to deny that the creator ever forgave sins, it is consequent to show that neither did he predict such a thing about his Christ: and thus you will prove this new kindness of Christ, if you prove it is not equal to the creator nor predicted by the creator. But also, can it be his to forgive sins, who is denied to hold, and can it be his to absolve, whose it is not even to condemn, and does it fit for him to pardon, in whom nothing has been admitted, as we have already discussed elsewhere.

pass_b_english: A paralytic is healed in front of a crowd, with everyone watching, and this miracle is a fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy that people will see the Lord's majesty and God's glory (Isaiah 1:18). So what's this majesty and glory all about? It's about being made strong, having your hands and knees freed from paralysis - that's what it means to be healed. And when Jesus says 'be strong, don't fear', he's not just repeating empty words or tacking on a meaningless caveat. He's promising that with physical healing comes a renewed sense of inner strength, so you can stand up, pick up your mat, and face your critics without fear, even when they question who has the power to forgive sins - a power that belongs to God alone. This healing is a specific example of the prophesied medicine, and it's accompanied by the forgiveness of sins, which is a central part of Christ's mission. In fact, the prophet Isaiah says that God will forgive sins and wipe them away, a promise that's repeated throughout the scriptures, including in the words of the Lord himself: if your sins are as red as scarlet, I'll make them white as snow, and if they're as red as crimson, I'll make them white as wool (Isaiah 1:18). The same message of forgiveness is echoed by Micah, who asks, what God is like ours, who takes away sins and forgives injustices, showing mercy and compassion instead of anger (Micah 7:18-19)? This kind of forgiveness is not just a New Testament concept, but it's also seen in the Old Testament, where God forgives the sins of the Ninevites, and where prophets like Nathan forgive sins, like David's sin against Uriah, and where King Ahab and Jonathan, the son of Saul, receive forgiveness through repentance. Time and again, we see God's people being restored through forgiveness, because God prefers mercy over sacrifice and repentance over punishment. So if you deny that the creator ever forgives sins, then you must also show that Christ didn't predict such forgiveness, and that would mean Christ's kindness is something new and unprecedented - but if you look at the scriptures, you'll see that's just not true. And let's not forget the question of whether Christ can even forgive sins in the first place, given that he's not recognized as the one who holds the power to condemn or forgive - it's a question we've discussed elsewhere, but it's worth repeating: can Christ really pardon sins if he's not acknowledged as the one with the authority to do so?

review.notes: Pass B is a paraphrase/summary rather than a translation and fails the completeness and fidelity requirements. Specifically, Pass B adds significant interpretive commentary and external scripture citations not present in the Locked Latin, such as '(Isaiah 1:18)' and '(Micah 7:18-19)', and introduces phrases like 'this miracle is a fulfillment of...' and 'a power that belongs to God alone' which are not in the source. Furthermore, Pass B fails to accurately translate the specific logic of the final sentence: the Latin 'cuius non sit etiam damnare' (whose it is not even to condemn) is rendered in Pass B as 'given that he's not recognized as the one who holds the power to condemn or forgive', which shifts the agency and modality of the argument. Pass A is a much closer translation but Pass B's failure to adhere to the source text as a translation makes the pair fail.
reasons: Pass B is a paraphrase/summary that adds interpretive content and external citations not found in the Locked Latin, such as 'this miracle is a fulfillment of...' and '(Isaiah 1:18)'. It also alters the meaning of the final clause 'cuius non sit etiam damnare' by adding interpretive framing not present in the source.

The translation fails to preserve the original meaning of 'paralyticus' as 'paralytic' and instead uses 'a paralytic is healed' which is correct, but the phrase 'in front of a crowd, with everyone watching' is not in the source text. The source says 'in coetu, spectante populo' which means 'in a gathering, with the people watching,' not 'in front of a crowd, with everyone watching.'

The translation incorrectly cites 'Isaiah 1:18' for the quote 'if your sins are like scarlet, I will whiten them like snow,' but the source text says 'etsi fuerint delicta uestra tamquam roseum, uelut niuem exalbabo, etsi tamquam coccinum, uelut lanam exalbabo,' which is not the same as Isaiah 1:18. The source text is a paraphrase of Isaiah 1:18, but the citation is incorrect.

The translation incorrectly cites 'Micah 7:18-19' for the quote 'what God is like you? taking away iniquities and passing over injustices to the remnant of your inheritance,' but the source text says 'quis deus, quomodo tu? eximens iniquitates et praeteriens iniustitias residuis hereditatis tuae;' which is not the same as Micah 7:18-19. The source text is a paraphrase of Micah 7:18-19, but the citation is incorrect.
